title: Gatherings that last (Avot 4:11)
hookLine: a group chat splitting into side chats: Yochanan the sandal-maker says every gathering for heaven's sake will endure
tomorrow: you embarrassed someone younger in front of everyone. now what?

cards: First the main group chat goes quiet. Then the side chats start. Two people who were friends last month now leave a room when the other walks in.
Somebody says: we need a meeting. And somebody else says: we need a meeting so I can tell them exactly what they did. Same word, two different meetings.
Which one actually lasts? A sage who made sandals for a living answered that.

teach.b: His name in the Mishnah is Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, Yochanan the sandal-maker, a sage known by his trade. Here's his saying, in plain words.
Every gathering that is for the sake of heaven will endure in the end. And one that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure in the end. For the sake of heaven, l'shem shamayim, is the key.
It doesn't mean the meeting has to be about God, or held in a synagogue. It means the gathering is for something bigger than the people in it.

teach.h: NOT FOR WINNING. FOR THE THING.
teach.b: Not for my side winning. Not for being proved right. For the thing itself: the show, the family, the truth, the person who's hurting.
Here's where it helps this week.
Before you call people together, ask what the gathering is for. If the honest answer is to win, it may still happen, and it may even feel good, but in this saying it doesn't last.

If the answer is the shared thing, people can disagree hard and still walk out together. The sandal-maker isn't promising calm meetings. He's promising that the purpose decides what's left standing afterward.

how: Jewish study, prayer and community meetings often open by naming their purpose, and some groups dedicate a session l'shem shamayim or in someone's memory before they begin.

o: a gathering for a purpose beyond its members endures
only meetings held in a synagogue are kept by God
the longest meetings are the ones that matter most

games.q: the sandal-maker's saying — tap the pairs.
p: it will endure in the end
it won't endure in the end
for something bigger than the people in it

s: a gathering is only for heaven's sake if it's about God or in a synagogue
it means for something bigger than the people in it: the shared thing, not winning.
the saying promises that good-purpose meetings will be calm
people can disagree hard; the promise is that the purpose decides what lasts.
Yochanan is named in the Mishnah by his trade

games.q: your family's planning a reunion, and your two uncles want it at their own houses. you're asked to set up the call. what do you write first?
o: what the reunion is for: getting everyone together, before anyone picks a house.
the pros and cons of each house, so the stronger case can win fairly.
nothing; skip the call so nobody fights and the plan can wait.
games.why: for heaven's sake means for the shared thing. naming the purpose first doesn't end the disagreement, but it's what lets the gathering last.

practice: Think of one group you're part of that could use getting together: a team, a family, a few friends.

Version a short text inviting them, and before you write when or where, write what it's for in one line, something bigger than anyone in it. Read the line back slowly, and hold off on sending until the sit is done.

wordCard.voice: Gatherings that last. Yochanan the sandal-maker: every gathering for the sake of heaven will endure, and one that isn't, won't.

orig.note: Hebrew: for the sake of heaven, for a purpose beyond yourself.

carryVoice: Pocket this: for heaven's sake endures, even when the meeting is loud. Thirty-four of sixty; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:11 (Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar: every gathering for the sake of heaven will endure)
Mishnah Avot 5:17 (a dispute for the sake of heaven will endure; mentioned only in the trapdoor)
